title: Hello, what's your name?
title_target: Сайн байна уу? Таны нэр хэн бэ?
goal: Greet people, introduce yourself, and ask how someone is — while mastering the one verb that turns up in almost every Mongolian sentence: *байх*.
bekal: say hello and goodbye the right way, formally or casually
give your name, job, and where you're from using *байна*
choose between *та* and *чи* without offending anyone

dialogs.title: Яриа — Анхны уулзалт
dialogs.intro: Budi has just arrived in Ulaanbaatar for a semester as an exchange student. In a corridor on campus he runs into Сарнай.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Fine, thank you. What's your name?
lines.literal: good, thanks. your name who Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: My name is Budi. What's your name?
lines.literal: my name Budi. your name who Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: I'm Sarnai. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Oh, how interesting! Are you a student?
lines.literal: oh, interesting thing is! you student Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. Are you a student too?
lines.literal: yes, I student. you too also student Q?

lines.id: No, I'm a teacher. I teach Mongolian.

notes: ⚠️ **Сайн байна уу? is not a real question.** Literally it's "is it good?", but it works exactly like "hello" — you answer by repeating the same phrase, not by telling your news. The safest answer is one word: *Сайн.*

**Байна means "there is", "to be (somewhere)", and "is" all at once.** It's the busiest verb in Mongolian, and it always stands **at the end of the sentence**. Notice that in nine of the sixteen lines of this dialogue, the last word is *байна*.

**Баяртай literally means "with joy".** The word *баяр* means joy or celebration, and the suffix *-тай* means "with". You'll meet that suffix again in Unit 15, where it becomes the Mongolian way of saying "to have".
**Тийм = yes, үгүй = no.** ⚠️ To negate a noun, Mongolians usually use *биш*: *Би багш **биш**.* (I'm not a teacher.) *Үгүй* is used as a stand-alone answer.
**Ч бас means "too, also".** The two words almost always come as a pair, placed after the word they mark: *Та **ч бас** оюутан уу?* — "Are **you** a student **too**?"

grammars.title: Байх — the verb you'll use most
body: English always needs "am/is/are" ("I am a student"). Mongolian drops it in **self-introduction sentences** — but uses *байна* as soon as the sentence describes existence, a state, or something going on right now.
And here's the first gift: **the form never changes with the subject.** One word covers everybody.
after: Five lines, one verb form. Compare English, which needs *am/are/is*, or Russian, which has six forms per verb. **Mongolian leaves all that to the pronoun.**

⚠️ In simple introductions — name, job, nationality — *байна* can be left out: *Би оюутан.* is complete and natural. Adding it (*Би оюутан байна.*) sounds like "I am currently being a student" and is a bit odd.

grammars.title: Та or чи? A choice you have to get right
body: Mongolian has two words for "you", and picking the wrong one is a social mistake, not a grammar mistake. The rule is stricter than with French *vous*/*tu*.

head: Word
Say it
Used with
English equivalent
rows: older people, superiors, teachers, people you've just met, anyone in a formal setting
close friends your own age, younger siblings, children

after: **The practical rule fits on one line: use *та* until the other person switches to *чи* themselves.** Using *та* with a friend your age only sounds a bit stiff; using *чи* with an older person sounds rude. The risks aren't equal, so the choice is clear.
⚠️ Note that *та* is used even for **one** person. It isn't a plural form — the plural is *та нар*. That's different from Russian and French, where the polite form and the plural are the same word.

rows: To anyone who isn't a close friend. Safest.
To friends your age. Short form.
At the office and in shops.

⚠️ Only when parting to go to sleep.
The most common way to say goodbye.
Warmer, when you really will meet again.
Said by the one staying to the one leaving.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note that the last two phrases **can't be swapped**. *Сайн яваарай* is said by the person **staying**, and the person leaving answers *Сайн сууж байгаарай* ("stay well"). It works like "safe travels!" and "take care!" — and saying them the wrong way round sounds instantly funny.

blocks.title: Asking how someone is
items: *Сайн байна уу?* — How are you? The most common, and it also means "hello".
*Юу байна?* — What's up? How's it going? ⚠️ Very casual, close friends only.
*Сайн, баярлалаа.* — Fine, thanks. *Их сайн.* — Very well.
*Тэгэх юм.* — So-so, nothing special. ⚠️ An honest answer you hear a lot; Mongolians don't feel obliged to say "fine".

sections.title: Asking questions with уу and вэ

blocks.text: Mongolian marks a question at the **end** of the sentence, not the beginning. The word order before it doesn't change at all — no swapping like English "you are" → "are you".

head: Question type
Particle
Example
Meaning
rows: With a question word, after *н, л, м, в* and vowels
With a question word, after other consonants

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Don't forget the particle.** *Та багш* without *уу* is a statement ("You're a teacher"), not a question. Rising intonation alone isn't enough in Mongolian — accept this early, because in casual English "You're a teacher?" works fine.

Choosing between *вэ* and *бэ* is fiddly at first, but the test is simple: **say the sentence out loud.** *Хэн бэ* flows; *хэн вэ* stumbles. *Хаана вэ* flows; *хаана бэ* stumbles. Your mouth will choose correctly before your brain remembers the rule.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Зүгээр does three jobs at once
items: **"Not bad, so-so"** — answering "how are you": *Сайн байна уу?* — *Зүгээр.*
All three are the same word. Context tells them apart, and the context is never ambiguous.

blocks.text: The last sentence in that table is worth memorizing today. Mongolians who meet a foreigner almost always assume Mongolian is too hard to learn and switch straight to English or sign language. Saying *би монгол хэл сурч байна* is the politest way to ask them to stay in Mongolian — and it is almost always met with a genuine smile.
